SRINAGAR: The first consignment of Ladakh-grown Lilium flowers was dispatched to major flower markets in India on Tuesday, in what the Union Territory administration called a major step towards boosting new economic opportunities and entrepreneurship in the cold desert.The consignment comprised 15,000 red, pink, white, and orange Lilium blooms cultivated at an altitude of 10,600ft at the world’s highest flower field at Choglamsar, Leh. These “A-grade” Liliums have four to five buds on each stem and fetch a premium price of around Rs 150-200 in retail markets. The flowers, with a shelf life of five to seven days, will be sold in various domestic markets, primarily Delhi, Mumbai, and Chandigarh.Ladakh lieutenant governor Vinai Kumar Saxena, who flagged off the consignment at Leh airport, said: “This first-of-its-kind high-altitude commercial floriculture project in Ladakh represents a major agricultural and visual shift for the region, which has, since ages, been identified by its rugged mountains and barren valleys. Millions of Liliums have added a vibrant contrast to this dull landscape.”Saxena said the “historic” initiative had emerged as a powerful economic tool for creating alternative sustainable livelihoods in Ladakh.Fifteen women cut, sort and package the flowers at these fields for a daily wage of Rs 900 each. A young, qualified botanist markets the produce to flower markets across the nation. The employees are all locals.The UT administration has directed deputy commissioners of Kargil, Drass, Sham, Changthang and Zanskar districts to replicate the high-altitude floriculture model by identifying at least 20 acres of land in each district.The flower field in Leh, which houses more than 25 lakh blooms, was developed and readied within just two months. It was opened to the public on Sept 17 this year and has since received an overwhelming response from visitors.
Article Summary: The consignment comprised 15,000 red, pink, white, and orange Lilium blooms cultivated at the world’s highest flower field at Choglamsar, Leh. The flowers, with a shelf life of five to seven days, will be sold in various domestic markets, primarily Delhi, Mumbai, and Chandigarh.

Article Title: Can’t deny employee security clearance based on kin’s antecedents: J&K high court
Article Text:
The committee said CID’s denial of security clearance was not based on any adverse material concerning his conduct, integrity, character or antecedents but stemmed exclusively from 'the alleged antecedents of his brother and the perceived possibility of a security risk arising therefrom'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

SRINAGAR: A Jammu and Kashmir high court (HC) panel Tuesday rejected a CID report against an HC staffer, observing that an employee cannot be denied security clearance solely because of his brother’s alleged antecedents.HC engaged Pampore resident Firdous Ahmad Sheikh as a daily-rated worker on April 1, 2010, and posted him at its Srinagar wing. On July 4, 2024, HC regularised his services as an orderly under the Regularization of Services of Daily Wagers in the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh Regulations, 2022.Like other appointments, Firdous’s regularisation was subject to CID verification, as is required for govt employment in J&K. On Jan 1, 2026, CID denied him security clearance, citing the “heightened adversity of his brother, Abdul Qayoom Sheikh”.The matter was placed before the Chief Justice, who referred it to the Committee for Appointment and Promotion of Officials, Officers of the High Court Staff, for consideration.The committee verified Firdous’s testimonials and found them genuine. It said CID’s denial of security clearance was not based on any adverse material concerning his conduct, integrity, character or antecedents but stemmed exclusively from “the alleged antecedents of his brother and the perceived possibility of a security risk arising therefrom”.The panel said Firdous had served the HC since 2010, and nothing adverse had been reported about his conduct, integrity or performance. “On the contrary, the record reflects that his work and conduct have remained satisfactory and that no vigilance enquiry or complaint is pending against him,” it said.Quoting J&K HC’s Feb 11, 2025 judgment in the Mohd Amir Malik v. Union of India and others case—which held that a person cannot be deprived of his legal or service rights solely on account of the conduct or antecedents of his relatives—the panel noted that liability cannot be fastened upon an individual merely on account of the alleged acts or antecedents of a close relative in the absence of any cogent material establishing the individual’s own involvement, association, complicity or misconduct.
Article Summary: HC engaged Pampore resident Firdous Ahmad Sheikh as a daily-rated worker on April 1, 2010. On Jan 1, 2026, CID denied him security clearance, citing the “heightened adversity of his brother, Abdul Qayoom Sheikh’ The matter was placed before the Chief Justice, who referred it to the Committee for Appointment and Promotion of Officials, Officers of the High Court Staff.

Article Title: 25,000 crash victims treated under PM-RAHAT; hospitals reimbursed in 13,000 cases
Article Text:
PM-RAHAT provides care to 25,000 crash victims (PTI file photo)

NEW DELHI: In the past eight months, nearly 25,000 road crash victims have been treated under PM-RAHAT, govt’s cashless scheme, and in nearly 13,000 cases, hospitals have been reimbursed for cost of treatment, a top road transport ministry official said Tuesday.Speaking at a roundtable on “Rethinking Urban Speed” organised by Road Safety Network, additional secretary in road transport ministry Mahmood Ahmed said that the scheme has helped save lives. The scheme under Motor Vehicles Act makes it mandatory for hospitals to treat road crash victims for free treatment up to Rs 1.5 lakh per victim, subject to a cap of seven days from the date of crash. Different studies suggest that 50% of lives can be saved by providing quick medical care to road crash victims.Mahmood highlighted the need to strengthen electronic enforcement of traffic rules considering that there is a tendency to break rules and deployment of manpower to detect this can never be sufficient. “Unless there is a certainty of punishment, the deterrence will never come,” he said. The official said the system would work only if violations were detected and followed through.Experts and govt officials at the workshop observed that India’s growing vehicle-safety capabilities cannot substitute for controlling speeds on urban roads, where pedestrians, two-wheeler riders and cyclists remain exposed to crash and their severity is directly linked to speedChairman of newly set up National Road Safety Board (NSRB), Nitin Gokarn, said the nature of Indian urban roads compounds the problem as different users, including pedestrians, two-wheelers, cars, trucks, and others use the same space.It’s worse in congested areas where pedestrians have no option left than walking on the main road because pedestrian facilities are absent. What adds to their risk are wrong-side driving, inadequate medians and poorly lit road infrastructure.Gokarn said at times when segregation of vulnerable road users is not possible, there are cars and bikes on roads that can reach speeds of 240 kmph and 100 kmph. This makes them vulnerable and more so when the speed is higher, he said.Experts, at the meet, shared examples such as Paris which has a maximum speed of 30 kmph or less on 89% of its urban road network; Brussels-Capital Region has 86%. They added that speed management in Indian cities needs to move beyond the setting of speed limits and focus on the interaction between road design, enforcement, local conditions and the behaviour of road users.Prof Bhargab Maitra of IIT, Kharagpur said that speed management provides an immediate opportunity to improve road safety. “Speed management is doable, implementable and workable in the short term. It is not merely about reducing speed limits; it requires the right combination of engineering, enforcement and context-based speed regulation. Aligning road design, speed limits and operating speeds, while prioritising pedestrians, cyclists and two-wheeler users, can help make our urban roads safer and more inclusive,” he said.
Article Summary: In the past eight months, nearly 25,000 road crash victims have been treated under PM-RAHAT, govt’s cashless scheme. In nearly 13,000 cases, hospitals have been reimbursed for cost of treatment, a top road transport ministry official said Tuesday.
